files: temperature.csv (528,278 rows; daily min/max temps for ~6 BoM stations 1910-2019)
rainfall.csv (179,273 rows; daily rainfall for 6 cities 1858-2020)
majorIncidents-2020-01-06.json (143 NSW Rural Fire Service major incidents, snapshot 2020-01-06)
dataset.what_one_row_represents: varies by file: a daily city-temperature reading; a daily city-rainfall reading; a single 1km MODIS satellite fire-pixel detection; or one declared NSW RFS incident polygon
dataset.geographic_scope: Australia, with Bureau of Meteorology data weighted toward six South-East / coastal capital cities (Brisbane, Sydney, Canberra, Melbourne, Perth, Adelaide); MODIS covers continental Australia; RFS covers New South Wales only

ana_01.label: Capital cities have warmed 1.2-2.4 C since 1910-1940
ana_01.content: Comparing the 2010-2019 decade to the 1910-1940 baseline, every Australian capital with continuous records has warmed substantially. Canberra leads at +2.39 C (19.14 -> 21.53 C mean daily maximum), followed by Perth at +2.10 C (23.73 -> 25.82 C), Melbourne at +1.62 C, and Sydney at +1.17 C. Brisbane lacks pre-1949 data so cannot be compared on the same baseline; its 2010-2019 mean is 25.64 C. These are city-station maxima, not national averages, but the direction is unambiguous: every comparable city is hotter than it was a century ago by between one and almost two and a half degrees.

calculation.output: Canberra +2.39 C; Perth +2.10 C; Melbourne +1.62 C; Sydney +1.17 C; Brisbane n/a (no baseline)

data_table.description: Decadal mean daily maximum temperature by city — 1910-1940 baseline vs 2010-2019

ana_02.label: 2019 was the hottest year on record across the panel
ana_02.content: Pooling the five long-record cities, 2019 sits at 26.40 C — the highest annual mean daily maximum in the entire 1910-2019 window and roughly 3 C above the surrounding decade. The 2019 value is so anomalous that it dwarfs any earlier excursion in the series: the previous five-year average (2014-2018) was 23.31 C, and the early-record five-year average (1910-1914) was 21.64 C. The shape of the curve is gradual warming through the 20th century followed by a step-function jump in 2019, exactly the climatological pre-condition the Bureau of Meteorology described in its 2019 Annual Climate Statement.

data_table.description: Yearly mean daily maximum temperature, 1910-2019, pooled across Brisbane/Canberra/Melbourne/Perth/Sydney

ana_03.label: Per-city warming series for small multiples
ana_03.content: When the mean-daily-maximum series is broken out by city, every city shows a long-run warming signal but the slopes differ. Canberra rises from a first-decade mean of 18.61 C to a final-decade mean of 21.53 C (delta +2.92 C). Perth runs +2.41 C, Melbourne +1.57 C, Brisbane +0.90 C, Sydney +0.83 C. The 2019 value in every city visibly breaks above the prior decade's range, consistent with the national 2019 anomaly observed in ana_02.

calculation.output: Brisbane +0.90 C; Canberra +2.92 C; Melbourne +1.57 C; Perth +2.41 C; Sydney +0.83 C (first 10y vs last 10y)

data_table.description: Yearly mean daily maximum temperature per city, 1910-2019

ana_04.label: 2019 rainfall was 49-79% of long-term average
ana_04.content: Every city for which 2019 totals are available recorded substantially below-average rainfall. Brisbane received 654.6 mm — just 49% of its 1,333 mm long-term average. Canberra, the smallest amount in absolute terms, came in at 358.6 mm or 62% of its 583 mm average. Melbourne and Sydney each landed at 70%. Perth was driest only relative to itself, at 79%. Adelaide had no complete 2019 daily series in the dataset to score. The rainfall shortfall was not a small wobble: it was a roughly one-third to one-half drop across the most populated and fire-vulnerable corner of the country.

calculation.output: Brisbane 654.6 mm = 49% of avg; Canberra 358.6 mm = 62%; Melbourne 441.5 mm = 70%; Sydney 851.8 mm = 70%; Perth 550.5 mm = 79%; Adelaide n/a

data_table.description: 2019 annual rainfall vs long-term average per city

ana_05.label: Canberra's driest year on record was 2019
ana_05.content: Ranking 2019 against the full historical record at each station produces an even harsher reading. In Canberra, 2019 (358.6 mm) was the single driest year in the available 11-year station record. Brisbane's 2019 was the 5th-driest of 42 years, Perth's 5th of 52, Melbourne's 7th of 49, and Sydney's 19th of 161 — but every one of these falls in the bottom 12-15% of years on record. Sydney's all-time driest year remains 1888 at 583 mm, but that record was set by a 19th-century drought; 2019 ranks among the worst years of the modern era at every station the dataset can score.

data_table.description: 2019 rainfall ranking among each city's full station record

ana_06.label: Spring 2019 collapse — November and December were nearly bone dry
ana_06.content: The shape of the 2019 deficit was not uniform across months: it was a late-spring/early-summer collapse exactly when Australia's fire fuel finishes drying out. Canberra received 1.2 mm in December against an 84.7 mm climatology (-83.5 mm); Sydney 1.6 mm against 77.6 mm (-76.0 mm); Melbourne 4.4 mm against 62.3 mm (-57.9 mm); Brisbane 9.6 mm in November against 135.3 mm (-125.7 mm); Perth 2.6 mm in December against 10.0 mm. By contrast, March and June 2019 were near-average or wetter than usual at several stations — the 2019 drought was concentrated in the months that mattered most for fire weather.

calculation.output: Canberra Dec -83.5 mm; Sydney Dec -76.0 mm; Melbourne Dec -57.9 mm; Brisbane Nov -125.7 mm

data_table.description: Monthly rainfall in 2019 vs prior climatology for each city (selected southeastern subset)

ana_07.label: Pooled six-city rainfall in 2019 was 61% of long-term average
ana_07.content: Averaged across the six BoM stations in the dataset, 2019's annual rainfall was 571 mm — just 61% of the 931 mm long-term mean and the lowest pooled total in the recorded panel. The decline since 2010 has been almost monotonic: 2010 saw 1190 mm (a wet anomaly from the breaking of the Millennium Drought), then a steady decline to 2014's 769 mm, with 2017-2019 returning consecutive sub-average years of 731, 671, and 571 mm. The trajectory matches the BoM's official national finding that 2019 was Australia's driest year on record.

ana_08.label: MODIS detected 34,248 fire pixels in eight days
ana_08.content: Across the seven-day window 2019-12-29 to 2020-01-05, MODIS satellites returned 34,248 thermal-anomaly pixels over mainland Australia. Detections were uneven by day: 6,936 pixels on December 30, dipping to 3,246-3,702 on December 29 / 31 / January 1, jumping to 4,394 and 4,273 on the next two days, then peaking at 7,384 on January 4 — the day NSW and Victoria coordinated mass evacuations from the South Coast — before dropping to just 867 on January 5 (the dataset cuts off mid-day). The hot pixels were not random noise: they tracked the operational tempo of the disaster.

data_table.description: Daily MODIS fire-pixel counts over Australia, 2019-12-29 to 2020-01-05

ana_09.label: 62% of MODIS detections were graded high confidence
ana_09.content: Of the 34,248 detections, 21,318 (62.2%) carried high MODIS confidence scores (>80), 10,540 (30.8%) were nominal (30-80), and 2,390 (7.0%) were low confidence. NASA's documentation explicitly warns against using FIRMS data to estimate burned area, but the high-confidence majority gives reasonable analytical leverage on where the dominant detections clustered.

ana_10.label: Victoria contributed 59% of all detections
ana_10.content: Almost three out of every five MODIS detections in this window came from Victoria — 20,261 of 34,248 pixels (59.2%). New South Wales added 4,457 (13.0%), Western Australia 3,825 (11.2%), Queensland and inland scrub 4,138 combined, South Australia 1,227 (3.6%), and Tasmania just 340 (1.0%). The skew is striking given Victoria's modest physical size relative to Western Australia — and matches the press coverage of the East Gippsland fire complex (Victoria's south-eastern corner) being the single largest active front during this seven-day window.

data_table.description: MODIS detection counts and shares by approximate Australian region

ana_11.label: FRP distribution — most pixels modest, top 1% above 1.6 GW
ana_11.content: Fire Radiative Power on these pixels has a long, heavy right tail: the median pixel released 38.7 megawatts, the mean 125.3 MW (skewed by a few giants), the 90th percentile 266.8 MW, the 99th percentile 1,657 MW, and the maximum a single pixel at 7,109 MW. By bucket, 31.3% of pixels released under 25 MW, 42.6% sat in the 25-100 MW band, 20.5% reached 100-500 MW, and 5.6% — almost 1,800 pixels — exceeded 500 MW. The long tail is what produced the pyrocumulonimbus events Australian fire managers reported in this period.

ana_12.label: Highest-brightness pixels cluster in Victoria's alpine south-east
ana_12.content: The ten brightest pixels in the dataset all read above 506 K (the MODIS sensor's saturation), and almost all of them sit in a small lat-lon box in Victoria's alpine south-east — around -36.7 to -37.7 latitude and 147 to 149 longitude — corresponding to the East Gippsland fires that erupted just before New Year's Eve. The single hottest pixel, on 2019-12-29 at 15:40 UTC near (-37.74, 149.37), released 5,587 MW. These are not abstract pixels: they sit on the ridge lines and forested valleys around Mallacoota, where helicopters airlifted around 4,000 trapped residents and tourists off the beach.

calculation.output: Top 10 brightness pixels all 506+ K; lat -36 to -37, lon 147-149 (Victoria/SE NSW); hottest single pixel 5,587 MW at -37.74, 149.37 on 2019-12-29 15:40 UTC

ana_13.label: 60% of Victorian detections were after dark
ana_13.content: The dangerous hallmark of Black Summer was night-time activity: in Victoria, 60.6% of MODIS detections were night pixels (12,270 of 20,261). New South Wales ran 53.5% night detections. Most other regions sat closer to a normal day-skewed pattern (WA 26.6%, SA 14.3%). Night fire is operationally menacing — humidity recovery stops, crews fatigue, and the firefronts continue to advance — and the night-share data in this seven-day window confirms why Victorian and NSW agencies were unable to gain ground at night.

calculation.output: VIC 60.6% night; NSW 53.5%; QLD 41.3%; TAS 42.1%; WA 26.6%; SA 14.3%; QLD/NT/SA inland 27.8%

ana_14.label: Map of high-confidence fire detections
ana_14.content: A scatter map of high-confidence MODIS detections (n=27,049) shows a continuous arc along the southeastern coast — from East Gippsland in Victoria up through the NSW South Coast and as far north as the Mid-North Coast and Queensland border. Tasmania and Western Australia have visible but isolated clusters; the WA cluster runs along the Nullarbor coast; the inland centroid is sparse. This is a satellite-eye view of Black Summer's first week.

calculation.output: 27,049 high-confidence pixels; sample of 400 used for inline map

ana_15.label: 143 NSW major incidents on January 6 — 31 still out of control
ana_15.content: On the morning of January 6, 2020 — the day this dataset was downloaded — the NSW Rural Fire Service reported 143 declared major incidents. Of those, 82 were under control, 30 being controlled, and 31 still out of control. By type, 126 were bush fires, 9 grass fires, and a long tail of medical, transport, and storm-related incidents that show the RFS feed captured every active call, not only fires. All but 15 carried an Advice alert level (the lowest of three levels), reflecting the snapshot mid-week — the major Watch & Act / Emergency Warning escalations that defined the New Year's Eve days had subsided by the 6th.

calculation.output: Total 143; status: under control 82; being controlled 30; out of control 31; bush fires 126; grass fires 9

ana_16.label: Gospers Mountain alone burned 511,661 hectares
ana_16.content: The 15 largest NSW incidents in this snapshot read like a roll call of Black Summer's most devastating fires. Gospers Mountain, in Wollemi National Park, sat at 511,661 hectares — the largest single forest fire ever from a single ignition in Australian history (a lightning strike on October 26, 2019). Dunns Road, second on the list, was 313,536 ha and still officially out of control. Currowan, Green Wattle Creek, Carrai Creek, Badja Forest Road, Green Valley, and Little L Complex all individually exceeded 150,000 hectares. Across all 99 incidents with declared sizes, total declared area was 4.0 million hectares of NSW alone — out of the season's eventual ~24 million hectare national total.

calculation.output: Gospers Mountain 511,661 ha; Dunns Road 313,536; Currowan 303,648; Green Wattle Creek 274,068; Carrai Creek 238,602; total declared 4.0 Mha

ana_17.label: NSW alone declared 4.0 million hectares burning on Jan 6
ana_17.content: Of the 143 incidents in the snapshot, 99 carried positive declared areas. Their summed total was 3,996,859 hectares — about 4.0 million hectares burned by NSW incidents alone, with a median incident size of 3,572 hectares. Compared with the season's eventual ~24 million hectare national total, the snapshot already captured roughly one-sixth of the entire season's area within just one state, and well before the season ended.

calculation.output: 99 incidents w/ size > 0; sum 3,996,859 ha = 4.0 Mha; largest 511,661 ha; median 3,572 ha

caveats.content: Bureau of Meteorology data in this set covers only six urban capital stations (sometimes seven counting Brisbane variants). Trends are city-station trends, not nationwide regional means.
MODIS detections are 1km satellite pixels, not ground-truth fires; the same flame front is re-detected on every overpass. NASA explicitly warns against using FIRMS to estimate burned area.
The MODIS file ends mid-day on 2020-01-05; the apparent drop to 867 detections on Jan 5 is a sampling artefact, not a real fire decline.
RFS incidents file covers only New South Wales; Victoria's massive Gippsland fires are absent from that JSON and only show up in MODIS.
Brisbane temperature has no records prior to ~1949, so it cannot be compared on a 1910-1940 baseline.
